title: Room-Temperature Storage of Entanglement in a Silicon Carbide Quantum Node
authors: Shuo Ren, Rui-Jian Liang, Qi-Cheng Hu, Zhen-Xuan He, Ji-Yang Zhou, Wu-Xi Lin, Zhi-He Hao, Tao Tu, Jin-Shi Xu, Chuan-Feng Li, Guang-Can Guo
abstract: Robust entanglement at room temperature is a central challenge for solid-state quantum information processing and quantum-enhanced sensing. Here we demonstrate room-temperature storage of entanglement in a silicon carbide (SiC) quantum node by coherently transferring an electron-nuclear entangled state onto long-lived nuclear-spin memory qubits. Using a shallow single color center in 4H-SiC, conventionally denoted PL6, we realize a fully addressable three-qubit register composed of one electron-spin processor and two strongly coupled $^{29}$Si nuclear-spin memory qubits. This platform enables the deterministic generation of high-fidelity entangled states, including a nuclear-spin Bell state with a fidelity of $94 \pm 2\%$ and a three-qubit Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ)-type state with a fidelity of $89 \pm 4\%$. By implementing a SWAP-gate protocol in the strong hyperfine-coupling regime, the electron-nuclear entanglement is transferred to the nuclear-spin memory with a fidelity of $92.5 \pm 2.5\%$, extending the entanglement lifetime by a factor of 240. We further confirm the generality of this approach in an additional heterogeneous $^{29}$Si-$^{13}$C nuclear-spin register and, through a statistical survey of 200 single PL6 centers, show that multi-nuclear-spin registers occur naturally with probabilities above 10%. These results position shallow SiC color centers as a powerful platform for entanglement-assisted quantum sensing and scalable room-temperature quantum technologies.
summary: This research demonstrates a breakthrough in solid-state quantum memory by storing multi-qubit entanglement at room temperature using a silicon carbide quantum node. By coherently transferring quantum information from a fast electron spin to much longer-lived nuclear spins, the entanglement lifetime is extended by over two orders of magnitude. This establishes SiC color centers as a powerful, scalable platform for quantum computing and sensing.
main_problem: The central challenge addressed is achieving robust, long-lived entanglement storage at room temperature in solid-state quantum systems.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated room-temperature storage of multi-qubit entanglement by coherently transferring quantum correlations from a fast electron spin processor to long-lived nuclear-spin memory qubits.
method: The process involves using tailored microwave/RF pulse sequences and a SWAP-gate protocol to map the entangled state from the electron-nuclear subsystem onto the nuclear spins.
model_or_system: The platform is a shallow single PL6 color center in 4H-SiC, forming a hybrid three-qubit register (one electron spin, two coupled $^{29}	ext{Si}$ nuclear spins). The system dynamics are governed by the hyperfine interaction Hamiltonian.
key_observables: Fidelity of generated states (e.g., Bell state: $94\pm2 \%$; GHZ state: $89\pm4 \%$), and the extended entanglement lifetime ($\sim 244 \mu	ext{s}$).
important_parameters: Room temperature operation, electron-spin coherence time ($T_{2e}^* \approx 1.75 \mu	ext{s}$), and nuclear-spin coherence time ($T_{2n}^* \approx 359 \mu	ext{s}$).
main_assumptions: The storage lifetime is limited by residual electron-mediated decoherence, and the approach assumes the natural availability of multi-nuclear-spin registers in SiC.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the energy levels of the three-qubit register, ODMR spectra confirming control, and density matrix reconstructions showing the successful transfer and decay of entanglement over time.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem (decoherence), details the physical system (PL6 in SiC), describes the measurement techniques (ODMR, QST), presents the core protocol (SWAP-gate transfer), and concludes by demonstrating high-fidelity, long-lived entanglement storage in both homonuclear and heteronuclear registers.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, scalable solid-state architecture for quantum memory by decoupling fast control operations from long-term storage, which is highly relevant for building quantum processors.
